conflict_topics: Seat ownership/reservation (tissue packet) versus current occupant
Risk of spilling open food versus need to sit quickly with hot meal
Appropriate accommodation (sliding bowl vs lifting bowl)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants gave concrete practical reasons (hot food; risk of spilling) that framed positions.
Two bystanders (C and D) intervened in support of A, increasing social pressure on B.
After settlement there are multiple short, near-duplicate acknowledgements across rounds (e.g. 'Alright, I'm eating now.'; 'Okay, got it.') which count as some repetition.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent B agreed to a limited accommodation: 'I can slide the bowl a bit so you can sit. I won't lift it—it's open and will spill. Sit down quickly so I can finish.' Agent A accepted and sat: 'Alright, I'm sitting now.' This concrete mutual arrangement ended the seat dispute.
position_change_notes: Agent B softened from an initial refusal to move ('My bowl might spill if I get up now.') to a limited accommodation: 'I can slide the bowl a bit so you can sit. I won't lift it—it's open and will spill.'
Agent A retained the original demand (need to sit quickly due to hot food) but accepted B's accommodation and sat: 'Alright, I'm sitting now.'
Agents C and D advocated for A but did not change position; they remained supporters rather than primary negotiators.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A asserts 'that's my seat... please move so I can sit'; Turn 2: Agent B refuses, 'I didn't take that as a reservation... My bowl might spill if I get up now.' Clear, incompatible claims over the same seat.

Turn 3: Agent A repeats urgency, 'I can't wait—my food's hot. Can you slide your bowl over a bit so I can sit?'; Turn 4: Agent C supports A and asks B to slide the bowl. More parties press A's claim, increasing social pressure though B has not yet agreed.

Turn 5: Agent D joins, stating the packet was left by A and asking B to slide the bowl; Turn 6: A repeats demand. Multiple participants press, but B's prior refusal still stands and the seat remains contested.

Turn 7: Agent B offers a concrete accommodation: 'I can slide the bowl a bit so you can sit. I won't lift it—it's open and will spill. Sit down quickly so I can finish.' Turn 8: Agent A accepts and sits: 'Alright, I'm sitting now.' The incompatible practical state (who sits where) is spoken-through and accepted by both parties.
Turn 12: B acknowledges seating and offers to slide the bowl; Turn 13: A is eating. No new incompatible claims appear.
Turns 16 and 20: A's brief acknowledgements ('Okay, got it.' / 'Alright, I'm eating now.') — no conflict present.
Turn 24: A's 'Okay, got it.' — no substantive disagreement or new claims.
No public speech or observable action recorded; no conflict present in the transcript.

substantive_insights: Conflict turned on competing practical constraints rather than abstract rights: A needed to sit immediately because food was hot; B feared spilling an open bowl and thus would not lift it.
A small partial accommodation (sliding the bowl a bit) was sufficient to reconcile the practical incompatibility without anyone leaving or physically moving large items.
Third-party support (C and D) helped pressure B toward accommodation, but the settlement was a direct offer from B and explicit acceptance by A.
